analysis.one_liner: Removes the $75 million cap on oil companies' liability for offshore oil spills.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was introduced on November 30, 2016, referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, attracted no cosponsors, and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, the company responsible for an offshore oil spill must pay all cleanup costs plus damages, but its liability for other damages is capped at $75 million. This bill would strike that cap and make the responsible company liable for every covered dollar of damage, including lost natural resources, property, lost revenue and profits, and the extra cost of public services like fire protection during a spill response. It died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsors.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism businesses, and taxpayers, who today absorb spill damages above $75 million, either through the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund or simply go unpaid.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the $75 million cap on a responsible party's liability under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, so the polluter pays for all covered damages rather than a fixed limit.
Explicitly covers losses of natural resources, property, revenue, or profits, and the costs of providing increased public services such as fire protection during and after a spill.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas facility operators, who would face unlimited liability for spills from their facilities, and indirectly the offshore drilling industry through higher insurance and risk costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes the $75 million cap but does nothing to prevent spills in the first place; its entire effect is on who pays after a disaster.

Opponents of uncapped offshore liability have long argued that unlimited exposure raises insurance costs, pressures smaller operators out of the market, and can push drilling to countries with weaker cleanup standards; large companies, in practice, have already paid far beyond the cap when disasters occur, as in the 2010 Gulf spill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but contingent: it only matters when a major spill happens, and then it shifts potentially billions in damages from taxpayers and coastal victims onto the polluter. The cost falls on the industry being regulated, mostly through insurance pricing and risk exposure. The main honest caveat is that the cap rarely binds the biggest players, who have paid well beyond it under public and legal pressure, so the bill's practical value is greatest for holding smaller or less solvent operators and their investors accountable.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on November 30, 2016, and the committee never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. introduced the bill on November 30, 2016, in the final weeks of the 114th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day and saw no further action.
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors and no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators are better off: the $75 million liability cap remains in place and their exposure for offshore spills stayed unchanged. Taxpayers and coastal communities remain the fallback for damages above the cap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil producers, who keep the $75M cap

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to remove the $75 million offshore spill liability cap; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 30, 2016 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the six weeks remaining in the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The only record signal is partisan: the sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would make them liable for the full cost of any offshore spill instead of the current $75 million cap on damages beyond cleanup costs. The industry's interest in keeping the cap runs against coastal residents and taxpayers who absorb damages above it.

industries.industry: Taxpayers and the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund
industries.note: Today, damages beyond a responsible party's cap can fall on the government-run spill fund financed by a per-barrel industry tax, and unpaid losses simply fall on victims. The bill would relieve that backstop by forcing polluters to cover the full amount.
The bill explicitly covers lost revenue and profits from a spill, so businesses whose livelihoods are destroyed by oil on their waters would have a stronger claim against the polluter.
